title: DNA from Poop Helps Scientists Find New Homes for the World's Rarest Marsupial
summary: The Gilbert's potoroo, a critically endangered marsupial the size of a small rabbit, clings to survival in Western Australia with a wild population under 150. These nocturnal creatures are notoriously fussy eaters, relying almost entirely on underground fungi. But identifying their specific diet has long challenged conservationists — until now. Scientists from Edith Cowan University and the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions turned to an innovative, non-invasive technique: eDNA metabarcoding of scat, or feces. By extracting DNA from fresh droppings, they could pinpoint exactly which fungi the potoroos consume without ever trapping or handling the animals. 'Traditionally, researchers would go through undigested material in scats, but trying to identify fungal spores remained a challenge,' explained researcher Esme Quah. The team also analyzed scat from quokkas, quendas, and bush rats — species that historically shared the potoroo's habitat. They found significant dietary overlap, particularly between potoroos and quokkas. This suggests that areas where all three species coexist likely offer suitable food resources for potoroo translocations. The research is urgent. In 2015, a catastrophic bushfire incinerated 90% of the potoroo's core habitat at Two Peoples Bay. Fortunately, insurance populations had been established on Bald Island and in a fenced enclosure at Waychinicup National Park. Now, scientists seek a new mainland site. 'The search for new translocation sites is an important next step in the recovery of Gilbert's potoroo from near extinction,' said Dr. Tony Friend. Beyond saving a species, the work highlights the ecological role of mycophagous (fungi-eating) mammals. They are ecosystem engineers, aerating soil and dispersing fungal spores that form symbiotic relationships with plants. Protecting them safeguards entire ecosystems.
why_it_matters: The research proves that cutting-edge genetics can save species from extinction, and it teaches us that even a tiny, fungi-eating mammal is crucial for the health of an entire ecosystem—a lesson in biodiversity we cannot ignore.

background_read: The Gilbert's potoroo is named after John Gilbert, a 19th-century naturalist who collected specimens in Australia before being killed in an Aboriginal attack. It was thought extinct until a small population was rediscovered in 1994 at Two Peoples Bay Nature Reserve on Western Australia's south coast.

Marsupials are mammals that carry their young in pouches; potoroos are related to kangaroos but are the size of rabbits. In 2015, a lightning-sparked wildfire burned through 90% of the potoroo's core habitat, but earlier, conservationists had moved a handful of animals to Bald Island and a fenced enclosure at Waychinicup National Park, creating 'insurance' populations.

Edith Cowan University, named after Australia's first female parliamentarian, collaborated with the State's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions on the diet study. eDNA metabarcoding is a technology that reads all the genetic material in a sample—here, animal droppings—to identify exactly what an animal eats without capturing it.

Mycophagous mammals like the potoroo are vital because they dig and aerate the soil, and their droppings spread fungal spores that form symbiotic relationships with plant roots, helping the whole ecosystem thrive.

perspectives.description: Conservationists now have a powerful, non-invasive tool to identify new habitats for the potoroo, raising hopes for its survival. Local ecosystems benefit because digging mammals aerate the soil and spread essential fungi.

Translocations are a high-stakes intervention—moving animals to a new area can fail if food or shelter is inadequate, or if predators are present. The 2015 fire shows that even protected reserves are vulnerable to climate-driven disasters, and relying on insurance populations is risky when the entire wild population is so tiny.

eDNA metabarcoding is increasingly used in ecology to study everything from biodiversity in soil to the diets of reclusive species, providing unbiased data on food webs. Mycophagy in small mammals is an underappreciated evolutionary trait that drives nutrient cycling in Australian ecosystems.

A successful mainland translocation could pave the way for similar rescues of other critically endangered marsupials. The technique might also be combined with drone mapping and acoustic monitoring to create a high-tech conservation strategy that monitors translocated animals without human interference.
